title: Chains with character
subtitle: What a peptide is—and what Peppy's bead body leaves out.
objective: Identify amino acids, peptide bonds and sequence without mistaking a cartoon for a chemical structure.

panels.alt: Peppy stands by an easel showing a symbolic four-bead chain
panels.label: THE CAST
panels.dialogue: I’m Peppy. Each bead stands in for an amino acid.
panels.note: Beads are a visual metaphor, not atomic structures.

panels.alt: Peppy gestures to two short symbolic bead chains on a table
panels.label: THE LINK
panels.dialogue: The chain gets longer when residues are joined.
panels.note: Pegs symbolize peptide bonds; the chemistry does not work by snapping pegs together.

panels.alt: Peppy compares red-green-yellow and yellow-red-green symbolic bead chains
panels.label: THE TWIST
panels.note: Same symbolic beads, different order. Chemistry and context matter too.

depths.curious: A peptide is a short chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Peppy’s colored beads are a way to remember the chain, not a picture of its atoms. The order of beads is called its sequence.
depths.college: A chain has a defined order from its amino (N) terminus toward its carboxyl (C) terminus. A peptide bond links neighboring amino-acid residues. Short chains are commonly called peptides; the exact peptide-versus-polypeptide size boundary varies by context. The same residue composition in another order is a different primary sequence.
depths.mechanism: Primary sequence constrains chemical behavior but is not a stand-alone activity prediction. Side-chain chemistry, stereochemistry, conformation, modifications, solution environment and the biological target all matter. The cartoon neither encodes peptide-bond geometry nor N/C-terminal chemistry, so use an actual molecular diagram for mechanistic analysis.

metaphor: Peppy's sphere-and-peg body is not a molecular diagram. Amino-acid side chains differ chemically; peptide bonds are covalent amide links, not detachable connectors. Sequence can influence activity but does not guarantee a particular effect.
check_question: If two chains contain the same three amino acids in a different order, are their sequences identical?
check_answer: No. Composition is the same; the ordered sequence is different. That alone does not tell us what either chain does in a cell.
